name: RareBench
intro: RareBench是首个系统性评估大语言模型在罕见病领域能力的基准。它包含了多个罕见病患者数据集，并提出了一种动态少样本提示方法来提升诊断性能。该基准还对GPT-4与专业医生的诊断能力进行了比较。
task_type: 分类, 抽取, 开放式问答
intro_en: RareBench is the first benchmark to systematically evaluate large language models' capabilities in the rare disease domain. It includes multiple rare disease patient datasets and introduces a dynamic few-shot prompting method to enhance diagnostic performance. The benchmark also compares the diagnostic abilities of GPT-4 with those of expert physicians.

drawio_review_note: reviewed_at=2026-07-18; status=source-reconstructed-awaiting-independent-signoff. Primary evidence is RareBench: Can LLMs Serve as Rare Diseases Specialists?, KDD 2024, arXiv:2402.06341v2. The reviewed PDF SHA256 is f8755b27ca798c59d53ea1261a77108a97ea1b5cc8fc5104402f255775f8371e. The official chenxz1111/RareBench repository was cross-checked at revision 82a9d8ca86c983ad6b22c5092fbb5b05ec66a0b6. Dataset sources and counts are preserved exactly in cases/diseases order. Four public sources contribute MME 40/17, LIRICAL 370/252, HMS 88/39, and RAMEDIS 624/63, totaling 1,122 cases across 362 diseases after the paper's screening. The PUMCH EHR cohort contains 1,650 cases: 1,183 rare-disease and 467 common-disease cases. All personally identifiable information is removed; PUMCH physicians monitor cases before text upload, and low-quality records with uncertain or imprecise diagnoses or fewer than three relevant phenotypes are filtered. Task allocation follows the paper's ordered subset construction. Task 1 uses 87 EHRs across 34 rare diseases and contains phenotype extraction, general entity extraction, and general entity standardization. Task 2 uses 33 EHRs across ALS, PNH, and MSA with complete medical-history and auxiliary-examination information. Task 3 uses 527 EHRs across 77 diseases: 60 rare cases spanning 13 rare diseases plus all 467 common cases spanning 64 common diseases; models return the top ten diagnoses. Task 4 combines remaining PUMCH rare-disease records with all public cases for 2,185 cases across 421 rare diseases and asks for the top ten diagnoses. These Table 1 counts are not normalized, deduplicated across task semantics, or replaced with repository convenience counts. Knowledge integration for Task 4 uses the HPO hierarchy and disease-phenotype links from HPO, OMIM, Orphanet, and CCRD. The integrated graph contains 17,232 phenotype nodes, 9,260 unique rare-disease nodes, and 21,505 phenotype-phenotype edges. The paper modifies Node2vec-style random walks with phenotype information-content weights so specific phenotypes receive larger transition emphasis, producing 256-dimensional node embeddings. A patient's phenotype embedding is an IC-weighted combination, cosine similarity retrieves the most similar cases, and the top three form the dynamic three-shot prompt. Prompt and evaluation contracts remain task specific. Eleven API and open-source LLMs receive a rare-disease-specialist role in the basic zero-shot setting; GPT-4 is additionally studied with chain-of-thought and random few-shot prompts, while dynamic three-shot retrieval is evaluated for Task 4. Task 1 reports precision, recall, and F1: phenotype extraction and general entity standardization require exact matches, whereas general entity extraction accepts equivalent meaning. Task 2 reports recall separately for ALS, PNH, and MSA. Tasks 3 and 4 report top-k recall for k=1,3,10 and median rank, counting success when the gold disease appears in the ranked diagnoses. These metrics must not be collapsed into a generic Accuracy, Exact Match, or single F1 label. Because the four tasks have different sample scopes and metric contracts, the page-level metric, metric_en, scale, and scale_en fields are intentionally blank; one metric label or the former 1,197 count cannot represent the paper's multi-task benchmark. A separate human comparison uses 75 high-quality PUMCH cases across 16 diseases and five departments, with 50 specialist physicians from 23 Class-A tertiary hospitals; each case is diagnosed by four physicians. That study is a dashed analysis boundary, not a benchmark-construction filter. Release and license provenance are deliberately split. The article is CC BY 4.0, the official repository code is Apache-2.0, and the current Hugging Face dataset card for chenxz/RareBench at fixed revision 6f054e04071953ef2c1779b279074245f2ab398c declares apache-2.0. The pinned README SHA256 is 88f68edf095f04fd741bd012bc9ae3009c1cbb624b548bf3ef83188ac30922ce. The card records PUMCH_ADM as 75 cases across 16 diseases, while the full 1,650-case PUMCH cohort remains unreleased. Fixed data.zip SHA256 458ebbbd7b8f2975aa9c3a1773e9c1fb103563a291775b6fd5e979375ed1ab3c contains only four public JSONL files and no PUMCH_ADM. Fixed Task1 zip SHA256 021059237c9a7748f996b377d1436ca1e43354dad232ecd855cb8f6d692b2c42 contains public_PUMCH-87.json. The current card records RAMEDIS 624/74, whereas paper Table 1 624/63 is the paper-era count; the diagram preserves the paper count and explicitly marks this release drift. Hugging Face card terms are current-release metadata only and are not extended to the unreleased full PUMCH cohort or upstream source rights. The article license is not promoted to a dataset license, and the repository code license is not presented as governing patient data. The bilingual specs retain identical node IDs, types, sizes, positions, styles, complete edge tuples, and node-avoiding branch waypoints including the public-data path; primary construction and evaluation edges are solid, while source evidence, human comparison, repository, release, and license boundaries are dashed. English labels contain no Chinese text and Chinese labels preserve every count and limitation. This is source-stage evidence only. strict Draw.io/XML and runtime visual review are required next; formal assets and page fallbacks remain gated until independent reviewer approval. Existing drawio, arch, SVG, and PNG files were not regenerated and are not publication evidence for this source-stage step.
